questions.enonce_markdown:
'Obedience is better than sacrifice' Comment on the validity of this statement in relation to Saul.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** The saying 'to obey is better than sacrifice' comes from Samuel's rebuke of Saul in 1 Samuel 15. To 'comment on its validity' is to show how far the career of Saul supports the view that God values obedience above ritual.

**1. The context in 1 Samuel 15.** Through Samuel, God commanded Saul to carry out the ban against the Amalekites and destroy them and their possessions. Saul defeated them but spared the king Agag and kept the best of the sheep and cattle. When Samuel confronted him, Saul said that the animals had been kept to sacrifice to the LORD at Gilgal. Samuel answered that obedience is better than sacrifice and that rebellion is as serious as the sin of divination. Because Saul had rejected the word of the LORD, he was rejected as king.

**2. An earlier case in 1 Samuel 13.** At Gilgal, facing the Philistines, Saul grew impatient waiting for Samuel and offered the burnt offering himself. This was an act of disobedience to the command to wait, and Samuel told him that his kingdom would not endure.

**3. Evidence that the statement is valid.**
(i) The sacrifices Saul offered did not make up for his disobedience, because God desires a heart that follows His word.
(ii) Saul's excuses, such as blaming the people and appealing to sacrifice, showed that his obedience was only partial.
(iii) His confession was weakened by his concern for his reputation before the elders and the people.
(iv) The consequence was the loss of the kingdom and the withdrawal of God's Spirit, and later the tragic end at Gilboa.
(v) David, by contrast, is shown as a king who repented when rebuked (2 Samuel 12), and he was not rejected.

**4. The wider biblical message.** The prophets repeat the idea that sacrifice without a faithful life is empty, for example Hosea, who says that God desires steadfast love rather than sacrifice, and Amos. The Deuteronomic view of history links the blessing of kings to obedience to God's commands.

**5. Qualifications.** Sacrifice was not condemned in itself: it was part of Israel's worship. The point is that it cannot replace obedience. It may also be said that Saul acted out of fear of the people, which adds political pressure to his failure.

**Conclusion.** In relation to Saul, the statement is fully valid: his rejection resulted from disobedience, which no ritual could repair, and his story warns that worship is worthless without obedience.
